passage: Last week in our psychology tutorial I said, with full confidence, "Well, we only use ten percent of our brains anyway." Lavanya the expert. The words came out smooth, the way a song lyric does. Sarika, who sits next to me, turned and asked, not meanly, "Where's that from?" I opened my mouth and found nothing. Not a book, not a teacher, not a study. Just a feeling that I'd heard it a thousand times: in a film, in some advert, from my uncle at dinner. Our tutor smiled and explained that the idea doesn't hold up; brain scans show activity all over. I went red. What bothers me isn't being wrong. It's how true it felt, simply because it came so easily. Now I keep a note on my phone called "Things I'm sure of: source?" It's already embarrassingly long.

qa.q: What did Sarika ask Lavanya?
qa.a: "Where's that from?"

qa.q: What upsets Lavanya most about the tutorial moment, looking back?
qa.a: Not being wrong, but how true the claim felt simply because it came so easily.

qa.q: What new habit did Lavanya start, and how could it help in the next tutorial?
qa.a: A phone note called "Things I'm sure of: source?", which makes Lavanya check where a confident belief came from before repeating it.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt asking the question?
qa.a: Sarika seems curious rather than mocking, maybe unsure whether the question would embarrass Lavanya, and it ended up helping.

grounding: A student confidently repeats a familiar line about the brain and cannot say where it was learned.

passage: Mentor note on Aparna (intern, 21), week 3. Rukmini, features desk. Aparna filed a neat piece on storm season today. One line stopped me: "As we all know, lightning never strikes the same place twice." I asked where she had read it. She thought, then laughed. "Everyone says it. My grandmother, films, school." She could not name a single source, and she seemed genuinely surprised by that. She had typed it without a pause because it felt so obviously true. I showed her the weather office's page explaining how tall towers are struck again and again. She read it twice, went quiet, and then asked if she could check the rest of her piece for other "everyone knows" lines. She found two. My plan: pair her with the fact-check desk for a week. Her instinct to recheck is excellent; it just needs a habit behind it.

qa.q: Which line in Aparna's piece stopped Rukmini?
qa.a: "As we all know, lightning never strikes the same place twice."

qa.q: How did Aparna seem to feel when she could not name a source?
qa.a: Genuinely surprised. She had typed the line without a pause because it felt obviously true, and she went quiet after reading the weather office's page.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make after reading the page, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She asked to check the rest of her piece for other "everyone knows" lines and found two, turning one slip into a checking habit.

qa.q: How might the paper's readers have been affected if the line had gone to print?
qa.a: Readers would have seen a familiar myth repeated by a newspaper, which would make it feel even more certain to them.

passage: Thursday night. Okay, diary, I got caught out today. Kiran wanted to buy a proper tank for the goldfish we're getting for our room, and I said, "Why bother? Goldfish have a three-second memory. The bowl's fine." I've said that line maybe fifty times in my life. It rolls off my tongue like my own phone number. Kiran just asked, "Says who?" and I couldn't say. Not a book, not a teacher. It's just always been around, in jokes and cartoons and in Papa's voice. Kiran pulled up an article about goldfish trained to push a lever for food and remembering it for months. Months! I felt a bit stupid, and a bit sorry for every goldfish I've ever joked about. We're buying the tank. Tomorrow I'm checking three other things I "know", starting with bulls hating red. Baljeet

passage: Every Sunday evening, the small library above the ration shop in Chalakudy turned into quiz practice for the district contest. Jomon, twenty, was the team's loudest voice. When Avni read out, "Name a man-made structure visible from space," Jomon didn't even let her finish. "Great Wall of China. Everyone knows that." Avni didn't write it down. "Where did you learn it?" Jomon opened his mouth. School? A cousin? A poster? It had just always been there, like his own address. "It's famous," he said. "Famous isn't a source," Avni said, and pushed the old encyclopedia across the table, open at a page she had marked. Jomon read it slowly. The wall was long but very narrow. Astronauts said they couldn't pick it out. He closed the book. "I've said that answer at three quizzes."

qa.q: Where did the quiz practice take place?
qa.a: In the small library above the ration shop in Chalakudy.

qa.q: Why was Jomon so sure of his answer?
qa.a: He felt confident because the line came so easily and felt as familiar as his own address, so he took ease of recall for accuracy.

qa.q: Which choice by Avni turned the moment, and why did it work?
qa.a: She didn't write the answer down and pushed the encyclopedia across, so Jomon checked it himself instead of being told off.

qa.q: What might Avni have been thinking when she had the page already marked?
qa.a: She had likely guessed Jomon would give that answer and wanted a gentle way to show him, rather than argue.

grounding: A young adult repeats a famous claim he cannot trace, mistaking how easily it comes to mind for proof.

Ankita, you asked why I got so quiet in the seminar today. Okay. I'm Tenzin, I'm twenty, and I just found out I've been saying something wrong since, like, class six.
The professor asked for any myth about the brain, and before I could stop myself I said, "We only use ten percent of our brains." Full confidence. I've said it at parties. I've said it to my little cousin.
And she asked, "Where did you learn that?" And I opened my mouth and... nothing. Not a book. Not a teacher. It was just always there, like a song you know all the words to without knowing who sang it.
She showed us brain scans where lots of areas light up doing ordinary things. The whole room went "ohhh". I went red.
It came to my mind so easily. I thought that meant I knew it.

qa.q: What did Tenzin say in the seminar?
qa.a: "We only use ten percent of our brains."

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when the professor asked where the idea came from?
qa.a: Tenzin felt embarrassed and shaken, going red because there was no source, only a sense of always having known it.

qa.q: What could Tenzin try before repeating a familiar "fact" next time?
qa.a: Tenzin could pause and ask where it was learned, and look it up in a reliable source before saying it as true.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Tenzin's quiet mood after hearing this?

Tuesday. At the college quiz club, Parul laughed when someone mentioned pets. "Goldfish only remember things for three seconds. That's why they're happy in small bowls." Everyone nodded. Parul felt clever.
Thursday. Jahnavi caught her in the corridor. "The goldfish thing. Where did you read it?"
Parul opened her mouth. "It's... it's a thing. Everyone knows it." She tried to think of a book or a teacher. Nothing came. Just the sentence itself, smooth and familiar, like it had always been there.
Next Monday. Parul had spent Sunday night reading a science magazine piece Jahnavi sent. Fish trained to push levers, remembering for months. She sat on her bed, embarrassed. The sentence still sounded right in her head. That was the strange part.

qa.q: What did the magazine piece say fish could be trained to do?
qa.a: Push levers, remembering for months.

qa.q: Why did Parul feel embarrassed on Monday?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed because she had said the goldfish claim so confidently, yet could not name any source and the magazine showed it was wrong.

qa.q: What could Parul do the next time a line comes to mind that easily?
qa.a: She could treat how easily it comes to mind as a warning to check, and look for a source before saying it as fact.

passage:
Tarun, you said just now that lightning never strikes the same place twice. Let me tell you why that line makes me nervous.
I was twenty-one, on a trek in the hills with my college group. A storm came in fast. We were near a tall pine that had a black scar down one side. Somebody said we should move away from it. I laughed and said, "It's already been hit. Lightning never strikes the same place twice. It's the safest tree here."
Everybody laughed with me. I felt clever. I had no idea where I'd learned that line. Films, maybe. It was just in my mouth.
Our guide, a quiet woman from the village, didn't laugh. She made us all go down to the low bushes and crouch. Twenty minutes later, that pine was hit again. We saw it.
I'm Siddharth, and I still check where my clever lines come from.

qa.q: What was on the side of the tall pine?
qa.a: A black scar down one side.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he called the pine the safest tree?
qa.a: Siddharth felt clever and confident, without being able to say where the line came from.

qa.q: When the guide said to move, what choice in the story kept the group safe, and why?
qa.a: Following the guide down to the low bushes kept them safe, because she acted on real danger rather than a familiar saying.

qa.q: How might the guide have felt when the group laughed along with Siddharth?
qa.a: She was probably worried and firm, knowing the storm was dangerous and the saying was not something to trust.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young adult, the speaker trusted a familiar saying that could not be traced, mistaking its ease for truth.

passage:
With two minutes left to prepare for the inter-college debate in Kolkata, Bidisha scribbled her opening line: "Science tells us we use only ten percent of our brains, so imagine what education could unlock!" She had heard it all her life, from films, from a tuition teacher, maybe from a poster. It came so easily that it felt obvious.
Her teammate Usha frowned. "Is that actually true?"
"Everyone knows it," Bidisha said, pen already moving.
On stage, the other team's speaker smiled politely. "My opponent's ten percent line is a myth; brain scans show we use nearly all of it." The hall murmured. Bidisha's face went hot. In the corridor, Usha asked, "Where did you learn it?" Bidisha opened her mouth. She didn't know.

qa.q: What did the other team's speaker say about the ten percent line?
qa.a: That it is a myth; brain scans show we use nearly all of it.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when the other team called it a myth?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and caught out, her face hot, since she had never questioned it.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do before using a 'known' fact next time?
qa.a: Ask where she learned it and check a reliable source, even when time is short.

qa.q: How might Usha feel after having asked earlier whether it was true?
qa.a: Usha may feel frustrated and a bit sorry, having doubted it but not pushed.

At the aquarium shop in Delhi's Lajpat Nagar, Jasleen tapped the glass. "Don't feel bad for them in the tiny bowl, Manoj. Goldfish have a three-second memory. They forget the bowl every lap." She had said it so often that it came out like the time of day.
Her brother Manoj, who studied zoology, raised an eyebrow. "Who told you that?"
Jasleen thought. A cartoon? A school friend? A quiz show? She honestly couldn't remember. "It's just a fact."
The shopkeeper laughed. "Madam, my fish know feeding time. They wait at the corner at six every evening."
Jasleen looked at the fish crowding the corner and felt oddly unsure of something she had been sure about for years.

passage: Last Diwali, at my cousin's house, the uncles got into a debate about the economy, and I heard myself say, 'Well, you know what they say: India's youth are its biggest strength, and we're the fastest-growing everything.' Everyone nodded. My cousin Indu, who's doing economics, asked, 'Fastest-growing what? Where did you read that?' I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I'm Kamal, I'm twenty, and I'd heard that line a hundred times, on hoardings, in speeches, in forwards. It came out so easily that I thought I knew it. But I couldn't name one number or one source. It had just been in the air. Now when a line slides out of my mouth that easily, I stop and ask myself where it actually came from.

Tutorial note, Media Studies, Year 2

In today's tutorial, Raghav opened the debate with, 'Everyone knows breakfast is the most important meal of the day.' When I asked for his source, he said, 'It's just a fact. My mother says it, the TV says it, it's on cereal boxes.' His classmate Kamal pointed out that the last example might be the problem. Raghav laughed, then looked uncertain. I asked him to trace it, and by the end of class he had found that the slogan was popularised by food advertising decades ago, and that research on it is mixed. He said, 'I've heard it so often it felt obvious.' Next step: each student will bring one 'everyone knows' line next week and trace it to where it began.

Prof. Anand

qa.a: Tracing 'everyone knows' lines to their origin, which trains students to separate familiarity from checked truth.

passage:
Wednesday

Group presentation today. Simran asked why we'd written 'We only use ten per cent of our brains' on the opening slide. I said, 'Because we do? Everyone knows that.' She asked, 'Where did you learn it?' And I genuinely couldn't say. A film? A teacher? A poster? It was just always there, so easy to remember. We checked in the library. It's a myth, apparently. Totally wrong. I felt so stupid, because I'd said it confidently to at least ten people over the years. Simran was kind about it. She said, 'It's catchy, that's why it sticks.' That's the scary part. Catchy isn't true. I deleted the slide and wrote 'Where did I learn this?' on a sticky note above my desk.

Hansa

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after finding it was a myth?
qa.a: Hansa felt stupid and embarrassed, having repeated it confidently to many people.

qa.q: Why is Hansa's sticky note a useful habit?
qa.a: It prompts a check on where a belief came from, since something easy to remember isn't necessarily true.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt pointing out the mistake?
qa.a: Simran was kind and understanding, noting that catchy lines stick, so she likely felt sympathetic rather than superior.
